Variola virus / smallpox

Smallpox is the archetype of a human-only pathogen whose archival record, vaccination history, and eradication campaign show how disease history can be written from both documents and virology.
Virus Agent: Variola virus Ancient DNA evidence Low origin confidence
Choose a pathogen; the view stays still until you change it.
Why this matters

Smallpox shows why origin, earliest evidence, historical spread, and modern control have to be kept separate: secure molecular evidence is not the same thing as a birthplace, while eradication depended on a well-supported human-only reservoir.

How to read uncertainty

Earliest evidence, hypothesized origin, historical spread, and modern distribution are separate claims. The map labels which kind of claim each geography layer represents.

Known / inferred / contested / unknown
Known

Variola virus caused smallpox, circulated only in humans before eradication, and was controlled through vaccination, surveillance, isolation, and ring vaccination.

Inferred

Viking Age genomes document extinct variola lineages in northern Europe, but this evidence does not locate the pathogen's true evolutionary origin.

Unknown / contested

Older pox-like descriptions are diagnostically nonspecific, and ancient DNA sampling is geographically uneven.

Reservoirs and transmission
Agent

Variola virus

Reservoirs

Humans before eradication; no known animal reservoir for variola virus.

Transmission

Respiratory droplets and aerosols in close contact; contact with lesion material or contaminated bedding/clothing.

Modern status

Eradicated in nature; variola virus remains only in declared high-security laboratory stocks.

Evidence desk

Variola virus / smallpox evidence

The deeper geographic origin of variola virus remains uncertain; Viking Age northern Europe is earliest strong genomic evidence in this profile, not a proven birthplace.

Earliest evidence: ancient DNA Ancient DNA: yes
Origin claim

Viking Age northern Europe evidence

Low confidence Earliest strong evidence, not birthplace c. 600-1050 CE ancient DNA; deeper origin uncertain

Ancient variola genomes from Viking Age northern Europe push secure molecular evidence earlier, but they do not locate where variola first evolved.

Uncertainty: The profile separates secure Viking Age genomes from older retrospective diagnoses and from any claim of true birthplace. Ancient DNA sampling is geographically uneven; older textual descriptions of pox-like disease are diagnostically nonspecific.

Mapped as

Viking Age northern Europe evidence

Earliest strong evidenceLow origin confidenceSource-backed

This layer marks the evidence location used by ancient DNA studies. It should not be read as the pathogen's true geographic origin.

What is unsettled
  • Do not equate earliest ancient DNA evidence with actual origin.
  • Do not treat every older pox-like description as a secure smallpox diagnosis.
Modern echoes
  • Smallpox eradication depended on reservoir ecology, vaccine delivery, surveillance, and political organization.
